strengths: The core architectural idea—decoupling modality-specific conditioning pathways (self-attention for vision, AdaLN for proprioception/task conditions, cross-attention for tactile)—is a clean and well-motivated design choice, validated by ablations (DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds/DECO.p) that isolate the benefit of the decoupled fusion mechanism from simply adding tactile embeddings.

The plugin tactile adapter is genuinely parameter-efficient (7.97M trainable parameters vs. 83–91M total, an order of magnitude less than full fine-tuning) while achieving the largest reported gains on contact-rich tasks, which is a practically useful result for adapting pretrained visuomotor policies.

The paper contributes a new bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset (DECO-50) with active vision and dense tactile sensing (1062 contact points), which fills a documented gap relative to existing datasets (Table 9), and is collected on real hardware with meaningful scale (50 hours, ~8K successful trajectories).

Real-world evaluation is extensive by robotics-paper standards (>2000 rollouts across 4 tasks with per-object and per-stage breakdowns), and the analysis thoughtfully distinguishes tactile-relevant tasks (waste disposal, assembly) from tasks where vision/proprioception suffice (pick-and-place, material sorting), providing actionable insight rather than blanket claims.
Detailed appendices document data collection protocol, training hyperparameters, and per-object/per-stage results, aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single custom hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands and a bespoke active camera/teleop pipeline); there is no evaluation in simulation or on a second embodiment, so generalizability of the architectural claims beyond this specific setup is unverified.

Baselines are limited to ACT and Diffusion Policy (plus a naively tactile-concatenated DP.t); despite the related-work section citing several recent tactile-VLA/visuo-tactile works (e.g., Tactile-VLA, VTLA, ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy), none are used as empirical baselines, making it hard to judge whether DECO's decoupled fusion is actually superior to other modern fusion schemes rather than just superior to a simple concatenation baseline.

Reported success rates are based on small trial counts per condition (e.g., 20 or 80 trials) with no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or variance estimates, so it is difficult to assess the statistical reliability of relatively small performance gaps between methods (e.g., DECO vs. DP.t on several sub-tasks).

The dataset and task suite, while a useful contribution, remain modest in scale and diversity (4 scenarios, 28 sub-tasks) relative to the scale needed to support claims of general applicability to pretrained VLA models; the paper's own future-work section acknowledges long-horizon and larger-scale VLA integration is unaddressed.

The theoretical justification for the central hypothesis ("different modalities contribute differently to action generation, hence require different injection mechanisms") is asserted rather than analytically derived or tested against alternative pairings of mechanisms-to-modalities (e.g., cross-attention for proprioception, AdaLN for tactile), so the specific mechanism-modality assignment in DECO is empirically supported but not theoretically motivated.

No explicit statement on code/dataset release plans, and the specialized teleoperation/hardware requirements (custom active camera, Vision Pro-based retargeting, specific dexterous hands) make exact reproduction by other groups challenging even if the dataset itself were released.

strengths: The paper contributes a genuinely large real-robot dataset (DECO-50: >50 hours, ~5M frames, 8K successful trajectories across 4 scenarios/28 sub-tasks) with simultaneous bimanual dexterous-hand, active-vision, and 17-pad tactile sensing, which is comparatively rare among existing bimanual datasets (Table 9 comparison is informative).

The architectural idea of routing different modalities through mechanisms matched to their statistical/temporal properties (vision/actions via joint self-attention, proprioception/task/time via AdaLN, sparse/noisy tactile via cross-attention with a LoRA-based plug-in adapter) is a reasonable and clearly described design, and the paper backs it with a real ablation (DECO.cs vs DECO.ds vs DECO.p) that isolates injection mechanism from training-from-scratch vs adapter effects.

The evaluation includes substantial real-world rollouts (>2,000 trials), per-object/per-stage breakdowns (Tables 2-4, 11-14), and an explicit categorization of tasks into weakly vs. strongly tactile-relevant, which gives a nuanced, credible narrative about when tactile sensing helps rather than a blanket claim.
Parameter efficiency of the adapter (7.97M trainable vs 83-91M total) is clearly quantified and supports the practical utility claim of plug-in tactile adaptation without full retraining.
weaknesses: All quantitative results are single-run success counts (e.g., 20 trials per object/stage) with no repeated trials, seeds, or confidence intervals/variance reporting; given inherent stochasticity of real-robot rollouts and teleoperation-collected data, several reported gaps (e.g., single-digit differences like DECO 37/80 vs DECO.p 55/80 on Assembly Stage set) could plausibly fall within noise, but this is never assessed statistically.

The empirical comparison is restricted to ACT and Diffusion Policy (plus a naive tactile-concatenation variant DP.t) trained entirely on the authors' own DECO-50 data; no comparison is made to the tactile-VLA or visuo-tactile fusion methods discussed at length in Related Work (e.g., ViTacFormer, OmniVLA, ForceVLA, Reactive Diffusion Policy), despite these being the most relevant prior art for the paper's central claim about superior tactile fusion.

The ablation intended to isolate 'decoupled vs coupled' injection (DECO.cs vs DECO.ds/DECO.p) is confounded: the coupled variant simply appends tactile embeddings to conditioning, while the decoupled/adapter variants use a qualitatively different and higher-capacity cross-attention mechanism, so the observed gains may reflect the cross-attention mechanism itself rather than the 'decoupling' principle per se.

All data come from a single robot embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands) and a single lab environment/table setup; no evidence is given that the decoupled-conditioning design or the tactile adapter transfers across embodiments, sensor types, or environments, which is a strong limitation given the generality claimed in the abstract/conclusion.

OOD generalization results (Table 12) reveal that the base vision-only DECO model degrades sharply on novel objects (e.g., 4/20 on 'Black Mouse OOD'), and even DECO.p, while better, is still far from robust (18/20 at best on one OOD case, with others untested for ACT/DP as baselines under OOD), suggesting the core architecture's generalization is fragile despite strong in-distribution numbers.

The claimed hypothesis that 'different modalities should influence the policy through distinct mechanisms' is asserted rather than theoretically motivated or tested against alternative decoupling schemes (e.g., different modality-to-mechanism assignments); the paper only tests the one specific assignment it proposes plus a naive coupled baseline, limiting insight into why this particular assignment is optimal.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: hyperparameters and dataset details are provided in appendices, but there is no explicit statement of code or model checkpoint release, and success/failure criteria for real-world trials are not rigorously specified (e.g., no inter-rater or blinded evaluation protocol described).

The Impact Statement is boilerplate ('none which we feel must be specifically highlighted') despite the work involving teleoperated data collection from human operators and deployment of dexterous bimanual hardware, which typically warrants at least brief discussion of safety or data/privacy considerations.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated decoupled multimodal DiT design that injects vision via self-attention, proprioception via AdaLN, and tactile via cross-attention with a lightweight LoRA-based plugin adapter, offering a principled and parameter-efficient way to incorporate heterogeneous modalities into a pretrained visuomotor policy.

Releases DECO-50, a sizable (50+ hours, ~5M frames, 8K successful trajectories) real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with active binocular vision and dense tactile sensing (17 pads per hand), which fills a gap relative to existing bimanual datasets that largely lack simultaneous tactile+dexterous-hand+bimanual coverage (Table 9 comparison is informative).

Extensive real-world evaluation (>2,000 rollouts) across four tasks of varying tactile-dependence, with strong baselines (ACT, DP, and a naive tactile-concatenation variant DP.t), plus fine-grained per-object/per-stage breakdowns (Tables 2-4, 11-14) that support nuanced claims about when tactile helps versus when vision/proprioception suffice.

Ablation studies (DECO.cs vs DECO.ds vs DECO.p) isolate the effect of decoupled tactile injection from simple concatenation and from the adapter's parameter efficiency, showing the adapter achieves comparable performance to full retraining while updating <10% of parameters (7.97M vs 83-91M), which is a convincing efficiency argument.

Results show consistent, sizeable improvements from the full DECO.p pipeline over baselines on contact-rich tasks (Waste Disposal, Assembly) while being roughly neutral-to-positive on tactile-light tasks, giving a coherent narrative about modality-dependent utility of tactile sensing.
weaknesses: All comparisons are conducted on a single self-collected dataset/task suite; there is no evaluation on any external benchmark or dataset, making it hard to assess generalization of the architecture and adapter beyond the authors' own setup and object sets.

Baselines (ACT, DP) are re-implemented by the authors with modified channel configurations to match parameter counts; while explained in Appendix B.1, this introduces some risk that baseline tuning is not as thorough as for the proposed method, especially given DP's surprisingly weak performance relative to published DP results in other papers.

The paper reports single-run success rates (e.g., 20 trials per object/stage) without confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, which is a common but nontrivial limitation for real-robot evaluations with relatively small trial counts per cell.

The 'decoupled' hypothesis (different modalities should be injected differently) is not rigorously theoretically justified; the ablations (DECO.cs/ds/p) provide empirical support but the design choice of which modality goes through which mechanism (vision→self-attention, proprioception→AdaLN, tactile→cross-attention) still appears somewhat ad hoc/engineering-driven rather than derived from a principled framework.

The tactile adapter's benefits are demonstrated only on the authors' own hand/sensor configuration (Inspire RH56DFTP with 17 pads); no experiments test whether the adapter generalizes across different tactile sensor types or robot embodiments, limiting claims about broad applicability.

Long-horizon task performance still degrades substantially at later stages (e.g., waste disposal Stage 3, assembly Stage 3), and the paper itself acknowledges this as a limitation without offering a solution beyond mentioning future temporal modeling work.

The OOD generalization results (Table 12) show a fairly large performance drop for most methods, suggesting the method's robustness to distribution shift is still limited, which somewhat tempers the significance of the improvements shown in-distribution.

strengths: Introduces DECO-50, a new bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with synchronized tactile sensing (1062 taxels/hand) and active binocular vision, covering 4 scenarios and 28 sub-tasks, over 50 hours/5M frames/8K trajectories — filling a genuine gap since most existing bimanual datasets lack simultaneous dexterous-hand + tactile modalities (well documented via the comparison Table 11).
Extensive real-world evaluation (>2,000 rollouts) with per-object/per-stage breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals, which is more rigorous reporting than typical robot-learning papers.

The decoupled conditioning design (self-attention for vision-action, AdaLN for proprioception/task condition, cross-attention for tactile) is clearly motivated and ablated: the modality-swap experiment (Table 7) convincingly shows that the specific pathway assignment (not just decoupling per se) matters, with dramatic performance collapse when tactile and proprioception pathways are swapped.

The plugin tactile adapter is shown to achieve performance close to full retraining (DECO.ds) while updating <10% of parameters (7.97M vs 89.41M), which is a practically useful and cleanly demonstrated result relevant to adapting pretrained visuomotor policies.

Reasonable effort to control for confounds, e.g., the supplementary ResNet-18 vs ResNet-34 ablation to check that gains are not solely attributable to a larger vision backbone, and matching baseline parameter counts (DP channel resizing).
weaknesses: Baselines are limited to ACT and Diffusion Policy; no comparison against more recent visuo-tactile fusion approaches referenced in the related work (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, OmniVTLA), making it hard to judge whether DECO's gains are due to the proposed decoupling scheme specifically or simply a stronger DiT-based backbone versus older U-Net/CVAE architectures.

Per-object/per-stage trial counts are small (10–20 trials), and many overall success-rate differences between DECO/DECO.p and baselines have overlapping or near-overlapping Wilson confidence intervals in the detailed tables (e.g., Task 1, some Task 2 objects), which tempers confidence in some of the finer-grained claims despite the large aggregate rollout count.

Evaluation and dataset are restricted to a single robot embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands) and a single tactile sensor modality (piezoresistive, normal-force only, no shear), which the authors acknowledge but which substantially limits claims of general applicability of both the architecture and the released dataset.

The ablation study for the core "decoupled vs. coupled" claim (Table 5) is conducted on only two object pairs within the assembly task, not across the full task suite, so the generality of the coupled-vs-decoupled conclusion is not fully established beyond the highlighted contact-rich cases.

The hypothesis that "different modalities contribute unequally and should be injected differently" is a design choice validated mainly via one pathway-swap ablation rather than a broader theoretical or empirical exploration of alternative modality-to-pathway assignments (e.g., testing image-via-AdaLN or task-condition-via-cross-attention variants).

No analysis of inference-time latency/throughput trade-offs of the added cross-attention/adapter modules, and no seed-level variance reporting for training (only single best-checkpoint deployment per method is mentioned).

strengths: Extensive real-world validation: over 2,000 robot rollouts across 4 tasks (pick-and-place, material sorting, waste disposal, assembly) with detailed per-object breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals, which is unusually thorough for a real-robot manipulation paper.

Release of DECO-50, a genuinely useful bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active vision (50+ hours, ~8K trajectories, 28 sub-tasks) that fills a documented gap in existing bimanual/tactile datasets (Table 11 comparison is informative).

Well-designed, informative ablations: the coupled-vs-decoupled tactile injection comparison (DECO vs DECO.cs vs DECO.ds vs DECO.p) and especially the pathway-swap experiment (Table 7, proprioception via cross-attention vs AdaLN) provide fairly convincing evidence that the specific modality-to-pathway assignment matters, not just the presence of separate pathways.

The plugin tactile adapter is a practically valuable contribution: it achieves performance close to full retraining (DECO.ds) while updating <10% of parameters, which is attractive for efficient adaptation of pretrained visuomotor policies to new sensing modalities.

Extensive supplementary simulation experiments across four independent public benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) show DECO is competitive with or exceeds several larger/pretrained VLA baselines despite substantially fewer parameters and no external pretraining, strengthening generality claims beyond the custom real-robot setup.
Reasonably detailed methodological and data-collection documentation (teleoperation setup, tactile sensor layout, training hyperparameters) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: AdaLN conditioning, joint self-attention, cross-attention for auxiliary modalities, and LoRA adapters are all well-established building blocks; the contribution is mainly their particular assignment to modalities, which is justified largely post-hoc/empirically (via the one swap ablation) rather than from a principled design argument.

Real-world baselines are limited to relatively simple/older methods (ACT, DP, and a naive-concatenation DP.t variant); no direct real-world comparison to more recent visuo-tactile fusion architectures discussed in related work (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, OmniVTLA), making it harder to assess whether DECO's decoupled design is actually superior to other tactile-fusion strategies, not just to naive concatenation.

Evaluation is confined to a single hardware platform, one dexterous hand, and one tactile sensor type (acknowledged as a limitation), so claims about the generality of the decoupled paradigm and the tactile adapter's transferability remain unverified across embodiments/sensor modalities beyond the additional simulation benchmarks.

Per-condition real-world trial counts are often small (e.g., 10–20 trials per object), yielding wide confidence intervals in several tables; some reported gains (e.g., in Task 1, or certain Task 2 objects) may not be statistically distinguishable between methods despite being described as improvements.
No indication of multiple training seeds/runs for the main real-world comparisons, so variance due to training stochasticity is not quantified, which is relevant given the modest sample sizes.

The pathway-swap ablation (Table 7) explores only one alternative permutation (swapping tactile and proprioception pathways) rather than a more complete combinatorial ablation (e.g., vision via AdaLN, tactile via self-attention, etc.), limiting how strongly the results generalize to support the broader claim that the specific decoupled design is optimal versus merely one reasonable choice among many.

strengths: Substantial real-world evaluation effort (2000+ rollouts across 4 task scenarios with 28 sub-tasks), which is rare and valuable in this line of work.
Release of DECO-50, a new bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active vision, addressing a genuine gap identified in the related-work survey (Table 11).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (DECO vs DECO.cs vs DECO.ds vs DECO.p, and the pathway-swap experiment in Table 7) that provide some empirical support for the core decoupled-conditioning hypothesis.
Parameter-efficient tactile adapter (<10% trainable params) shows a practically useful strategy for retrofitting tactile awareness onto a frozen pretrained visuomotor policy.
Supplementary simulation experiments on four external benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) attempt to demonstrate broader applicability beyond the custom hardware setup.
weaknesses: Code/Project Page/Dataset links in the manuscript are blank placeholders, which is a serious reproducibility concern for a paper whose central contribution is partly a dataset release.

The abstract claims DECO 'achieves the best performance across all tasks,' but this is contradicted by the paper's own supplementary results, e.g., DECO scores 0/80 on the Assembly task under DexJoCo rand-obj (Table 25), undermining the generality of the headline claim.

Real-world per-object success counts are often based on only 10-20 trials per condition, giving wide confidence intervals (explicitly reported in the appendix) that make many pairwise comparisons in the main text (e.g., DECO vs DP.t on individual objects) statistically inconclusive despite being narrated as clear wins.

The core architectural claim (vision via self-attention, proprioception via AdaLN, tactile via cross-attention) is motivated largely by intuition/hypothesis rather than a principled derivation, and the pathway-assignment ablation (Table 7) is conducted on only two object pairs within a single task family (assembly), which is a narrow basis for such a strong general design claim.

No direct empirical comparison to more recent specialized visuo-tactile fusion architectures discussed in the related work (e.g., ViTacFormer, OmniVTLA, Reactive Diffusion Policy's slow-fast fusion) despite these being the most relevant competing fusion strategies; baselines are limited to ACT, DP, and a naive concatenation variant (DP.t).

Evaluation is restricted to a single robot/hand/sensor platform (acknowledged in Limitations), and the additional simulation benchmarks, while broader, use different model configurations (e.g., added T5 encoder for RoboTwin 2.0) making cross-benchmark comparisons and overall generality claims harder to assess uniformly.

The Impact Statement is a boilerplate non-statement that does not address any specific considerations relevant to this work (e.g., teleoperated human data collection, deployment of dexterous hands with force/tactile sensing near humans).

strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated architectural principle—decoupling modality-specific conditioning pathways (self-attention for vision-action, AdaLN for proprioception/task-level conditions, cross-attention for tactile)—and provides a clear ablation (Table 7, pathway-swap experiment) that convincingly demonstrates the pathway assignment is crucial, with dramatic drops (e.g., 0/40 vs 29/40 on Stage 3) when pathways are swapped.

Extensive real-world evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts across 4 diverse bimanual dexterous tasks (pick-and-place, dynamic sorting, contact-rich waste disposal, and precision assembly), with per-object breakdowns and Wilson 95% confidence intervals, lending good statistical rigor to the real-robot claims.

The plugin tactile adapter is a practically valuable contribution: it achieves performance comparable to full retraining (DECO.ds) while updating <10% of parameters (7.97M vs 89.41M), a meaningful demonstration of parameter-efficient multimodal adaptation for pretrained visuomotor policies.

DECO-50 fills a genuine gap in the literature (bimanual + dexterous + tactile + active vision, real robot) as shown by the thorough dataset comparison table, and is accompanied by detailed collection/hardware documentation (tactile pad layout, teleoperation setup) supporting reproducibility.

The supplementary simulation results across four independent benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) with comparisons to strong published baselines substantially strengthen generality claims beyond the single real-world hardware platform, and the ResNet-18 vs ResNet-34 ablation controls for a natural confound versus baselines using ResNet-18.

Detailed failure-mode analysis (e.g., timeout vs. slip breakdown in UniVTAC, per-stage analysis in waste disposal/assembly) provides good qualitative insight into why and where tactile signal helps or doesn't.
weaknesses: The core empirical claims rest on a single hardware embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands) and a single tactile sensor type; while acknowledged as a limitation, this restricts confidence that the decoupled-pathway design generalizes to other tactile sensor characteristics (e.g., shear-sensitive sensors) or hand morphologies.

Some real-world success-rate differences, especially in Task 1 and parts of Task 2, are based on relatively small per-object trial counts (10-20 trials), leading to wide/overlapping confidence intervals, so several individual comparisons are not clearly statistically significant even though aggregate trends are.

The justification for the specific modality-to-pathway mapping is largely empirical/post hoc (motivated by the swap ablation) rather than derived from a principled theory of what modality property should dictate the pathway, leaving open whether the assignment used is optimal versus merely one workable configuration.
The DECO.cs (coupled tactile fusion) ablation is only tested on 2 object pairs in the assembly task, a fairly narrow basis for the paper's central 'decoupling helps' claim relative to naive fusion.

The extensive supplementary simulation benchmarking compares against numbers taken from other papers under possibly different training budgets/protocols (self-reported baselines), which weakens direct comparison conclusions and is not deeply discussed as a caveat.

Presentation could be improved: some architectural details (e.g., precise interaction between the adapter and LoRA within the same forward pass) are terse in the main text and require cross-referencing the appendix for full clarity.
